### Problem: Number of Substrings With Only 1s {#sec-cnt-p3-ones}

::: {.p-statement}
Given a binary string `s`, return the number of substrings whose characters are all `'1'`, modulo $10^9 + 7$.

For `s = "0110111"` the answer is $9$: `"1"` occurs $5$ times, `"11"` $3$ times and `"111"` once. For `s = "101"` the answer is $2$ (two copies of `"1"`). For `s = "111111"` every one of the $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ substrings qualifies.

Constraints: $1 \le n \le 10^5$, $s[i] \in \{'0', '1'\}$.

Source: [LC 1513 · Number of Substrings With Only 1s](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-substrings-with-only-1s/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Every character is `'1'`" is a predicate that **decomposes the array**. A run of `1`s is a maximal block bounded by `0`s (or by the ends), and a substring made only of `1`s cannot cross a `0` — so the set being counted is the disjoint union, over runs, of "substrings inside that run". Nothing else in the string contributes. That is the contribution technique of @sec-cnt-a1 with *runs* as the units instead of single slots: answer $= \sum_{\text{runs}} f(L)$, where $f(L)$ is the number of substrings of a length-$L$ string.

And $f(L) = \dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} = \binom{L+1}{2}$: a substring is a choice of start and end with $start \le end$ inside the run, i.e. an unordered pair drawn from $L+1$ gaps, or equivalently $\sum_{k=1}^{L} k$ if you group by length. For `"0110111"` the runs have lengths $2$ and $3$, giving $3 + 6 = 9$ — the sample, with `"1"` appearing twice inside the first run and three times inside the second ($5$ total) and `"111"` appearing only in the length-$3$ run ($1$). Compare with @sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs, where the pair condition was $i < j$ and the count was $\binom{c}{2}$: the $\le$ versus $<$ distinction is exactly the $+1$ in $\binom{L+1}{2}$.

The streaming twin of the same identity counts by **right end** instead of by run: if the cursor sits on a `1`, then every substring ending here that is all-`1`s starts somewhere inside the current run, so the number of new answers equals the current run length $r$; a `0` resets $r$ to $0$. Reading `"0110111"` that way gives charges $0,1,2,0,1,2,3$, which sum to $9$. Both formulas are the same sum re-indexed — $\sum_{\text{positions}} r_i = \sum_{\text{runs}} \binom{L+1}{2}$ — which is what "one pass, $O(1)$ memory" is allowed to cost here.

Finally, the modulus is a hint about size: at $n = 10^5$ an all-ones string has $\binom{100001}{2} = 5{,}000{,}050{,}000$ substrings, which is more than $2^{31}$, so reduce as you go rather than at the end.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Enumerate and test.** Two loops over start and end, `all()` on the slice. $O(n^3)$ literally, $O(n^2)$ if you break the inner loop at the first `0` — and it is the only rung that survives a change of predicate, so keep it as the oracle.
2. **Split into runs, close each with a triangle number.** One pass collecting the length of the current run, and when a `0` (or a sentinel) ends it, add $L(L+1)/2$. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space. The contribution view: every run is credited in one multiplication.
3. **One pass, counting the substrings that end here.** `run = run + 1 if c == "1" else 0`, `ans += run`. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space, one line shorter, and the version that extends to "at most one `0`" style questions (@sec-sw-a2).
:::

::: {#fig-cnt-p3-ones}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["index",        "0", "1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"],
                   ["s",            "0", "1", "1", "0", "1", "1", "1"],
                   ["run ending",   "0", "1", "2", "0", "1", "2", "3"],
                   ["run length L", "", "2", "", "", "3", "", ""],
                   ["L(L+1)/2",     "", "3", "", "", "6", "", ""]],
           colors={(1, 2): "cyan", (1, 3): "cyan", (1, 5): "amber",
                   (1, 6): "amber", (1, 7): "amber", (4, 5): "green"},
           cell_w=1.1)
V.show(draw)
```

Row 3 is the streaming rung: the number of all-ones substrings ending at each index, totalling $0+1+2+0+1+2+3 = 9$. Rows 4–5 are the run rung: the run `"11"` at indices 1–2 owns $3$ substrings and the run `"111"` at 4–6 owns $6$, so $3 + 6 = 9$. The two rungs disagree about *who* is charged and agree about the total — the same swap as @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum, now on runs instead of slots.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Enumerate and test

::: {.form-next}
Every $(i, j)$ pair, `all(c == '1' ...)` on the slice. Written honestly as $O(n^3)$; breaking at the first `0` makes it $O(n^2)$. At $n = 10^5$ it is hopeless, which is exactly the point of the next two rungs.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("ones", "scan")
    assert str(final) == "9"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def one_scan(s):
    ans = 0
    for i in range(len(s)):
        for j in range(i, len(s)):
            if all(c == "1" for c in s[i:j + 1]):
                ans += 1
            else:
                break                      # no longer substring works from i
    return ans


assert one_scan("0110111") == 9
assert one_scan("101") == 2
assert one_scan("111111") == 21
assert one_scan("000") == 0
assert one_scan("1") == 1
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long oneScan(const string& s) {
    long long ans = 0;
    int n = s.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        for (int j = i; j < n; ++j) {
            if (s[j] == '1') ++ans;
            else break;                     // a 0 kills every longer start
        }
    }
    return ans;
}
```
:::

#### Split into runs, close each with a triangle number

::: {.form-next}
Credit a whole run in one multiplication. The sentinel `'0'` appended to the string is what flushes a run that reaches the end of the input — the bug this shape is famous for.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("ones", "runs")
    assert str(final) == "9"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7


def one_runs(s):
    ans = run = 0
    for c in s + "0":                     # sentinel: flush a run at the very end
        if c == "1":
            run += 1
        else:
            ans = (ans + run * (run + 1) // 2) % MOD
            run = 0
    return ans


assert one_runs("0110111") == 9
assert one_runs("101") == 2
assert one_runs("111111") == 21
# the two credits of the first sample
assert [L * (L + 1) // 2 for L in (2, 3)] == [3, 6]
assert [len(r) for r in "0110111".split("0") if r] == [2, 3]
# a run of length L has C(L+1, 2) substrings - compare C(c, 2) for i < j pairs
assert [L * (L + 1) // 2 for L in range(1, 7)] == [1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21]
for _ in range(150):
    t = "".join(random.choice("01") for _ in range(random.randint(1, 24)))
    assert one_runs(t) == one_scan(t)
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long oneRuns(const string& s) {
    const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;
    long long ans = 0, run = 0;
    for (char c : s) {
        if (c == '1') {
            ++run;
        } else {
            ans = (ans + run * (run + 1) / 2) % MOD;
            run = 0;
        }
    }
    return (int)((ans + run * (run + 1) / 2) % MOD);   // flush the trailing run
}
```
:::

#### One pass, counting the substrings that end here

::: {.form-next}
The tightest form: one comparison and one addition per character, with no flush step to forget. `run` is simultaneously "length of the current run" and "number of answers ending here", which is the reason it needs no sentinel.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("ones", "stream")
    assert str(final) == "9"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def one_stream(s):
    ans = run = 0
    for c in s:
        run = run + 1 if c == "1" else 0
        ans = (ans + run) % MOD           # run new all-ones substrings end here
    return ans


assert one_stream("0110111") == 9
assert one_stream("101") == 2
assert one_stream("111111") == 21
# the per-position charges read off the storyboard
charges, run = [], 0
for c in "0110111":
    run = run + 1 if c == "1" else 0
    charges.append(run)
assert charges == [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3] and sum(charges) == 9
# the modulus is load-bearing at the top of the range
big = "1" * 100000
assert one_stream(big) == (100000 * 100001 // 2) % MOD == 49965
assert 100000 * 100001 // 2 == 5000050000 > 2 ** 31
for _ in range(150):
    t = "".join(random.choice("01") for _ in range(random.randint(1, 24)))
    assert one_stream(t) == one_runs(t) == one_scan(t)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int oneStream(string& s) {
    const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;
    long long ans = 0, run = 0;
    for (char c : s) {
        run = (c == '1') ? run + 1 : 0;
        ans = (ans + run) % MOD;
    }
    return (int)ans;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** $O(n^3)$ naive, or $O(n^2)$ with the break at the first `0`; $O(n)$ for both fast rungs, one character per step. **Space** $O(1)$ beyond the input — no table, no prefix array, no run list (rung 2 does not need `split`, which would materialise $O(n)$ pieces). **Width of the answer**: $\binom{100001}{2} = 5{,}000{,}050{,}000$ at the top of the range, so an `int` accumulator overflows (ceiling $2{,}147{,}483{,}647$) even before the modulus; take the remainder every step. In rung 2 the *product* `run * (run + 1)` reaches $10{,}000{,}100{,}000 \approx 10^{10}$, which no 32-bit type survives, so do the multiplication in `long long` before halving and reducing.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All `0`s: no run exists, answer $0$. Both fast rungs give it for free (`run` never leaves $0$).
- All `1`s: one run of length $n$, so $\binom{n+1}{2}$ — `"111111"` $\to$ $21$ (the third sample) and $10^5$ ones $\to$ $49{,}965$ after the modulus.
- A run that touches the end of the string: rung 2 must flush it. The classic slip is to add only inside the `else` branch; on `"0110111"` that reports $3$ instead of $9$ because the length-$3$ run is never closed.
- $n = 1$: `"1"` $\to$ $1$, `"0"` $\to$ $0$.
- **Debug tip.** A result short by exactly $\binom{L+1}{2}$ for one run means that run's flush is missing — on `"0110111"` the unflushed version reports $3$ instead of $9$. A result of $28$ on the same input means `run` is never reset on `'0'`, so the counter runs through the whole string ($1+2+\cdots+7$).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **$L^2$ or $L \cdot (L-1) / 2$ instead of $L(L+1)/2$.** Substrings allow $start = end$ (the length-1 substring), which is what makes the count $\binom{L+1}{2}$; a run of $3$ has $6$ substrings, not $9$ and not $3$.
- **Modulo only at the end.** Fine in Python, wrong in C++/Java where the accumulator has already overflowed. Reduce per step.
- **Forgetting the flush** in the run-based rung (see the edge case above) — the sentinel `'0'` or an explicit closing add after the loop.
- **Counting subsequences instead of substrings.** Choosing any subset of the `1`s inside a run gives $2^L - 1$ objects; contiguity is what buys the triangle number.
- **Not resetting `run` on `'0'`.** The current run length is a *local* quantity; carrying it across a `0` counts substrings that contain the `0`.
- **Using `s.split('0')` and iterating the pieces** is correct but allocates; if you do use it, remember that a trailing `'0'` produces an empty last piece and `len('') = 0` contributes nothing.
:::

**Variants.** Flip the digit and you have LC 2348 (zero-filled subarrays) — identical code with `'1'` replaced by `'0'`. Replace "all `1`s" by "at most $k$ `0`s" and the same ending-here charge needs a shrinking window instead of a reset counter, which is @sec-sw-a2. And replace "count the windows" by "sum their lengths": that is @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum again, with the cover count $(i+1)(n-i)$ instead of a run length.

- [LC 2348 · Number of Zero-Filled Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-zero-filled-subarrays/){difficulty="Medium"} — this problem with the digit flipped; watch the overflow.
- [LC 1004 · Max Consecutive Ones III](https://leetcode.com/problems/max-consecutive-ones-iii/){difficulty="Medium"} — "at most $k$ flips" turns the run into a window (@sec-sw-p2).
:::
